1: # MSM83C154 Mask ROM Analysis
2: 
3: Analysis of the 16 KB internal mask ROM dumped from an OKI MSM83C154
4: (8051-family) microcontroller. The dump is `romdump.bin` (16384 bytes, internal
5: checksum verified).
6: 
7: ## The chip
8: 
9: Markings:
10: 
11: ```
12: 79X1396
13: M83C154-42
14: ©OKI '80/85
15: JAPAN 94000
16: ```
17: 
18: | Line | Reading | Confidence |
19: |---|---|---|
20: | `79X1396` | The equipment maker's own part number. Mask-ROM chips are often marked with the customer's number. The `79X` prefix doesn't match any scheme found online. | Medium |
21: | `M83C154-42` | OKI MSM83C154 with ROM code 42: the number OKI gave this customer program. Based on OKI's suffix pattern; nothing confirms "-42" itself. | Medium |
22: | `©OKI '80/85` | Standard OKI copyright line, not a date code. '80 likely refers to the MCS-51 architecture, '85 to OKI's CMOS version. | Medium |
23: | `JAPAN 94000` | Probably date and lot. OKI's format isn't documented online. Most plausible: 1994, or 1989/1999 with a month and lot number. | Low |
24: 
25: Neither `79X1396` nor `M83C154-42` appears anywhere online (searched
26: 2026-11-23). The markings show the chip was made for one company's product
27: under its own part number. If 94 is the year, it is late for a mask-ROM 8051,
28: which would suggest a mature, long-running product.
29: 
30: Custom OKI MSM83C154s did turn up in communications equipment: a Hayes modem
31: used one
32: ([listing](https://www.electronicsurplus.com/oki-msm83c154-ic-hayes-copyright-p-n-04-00119-v2-5)).
33: This chip is marked differently, so that is not evidence of a Hayes
34: connection.
35: 
36: OKI's 1986 and 1988 microcontroller data books may explain the marking and
37: date-code layout:
38: [1986](https://bitsavers.trailing-edge.com/components/oki/_dataBooks/1986_OKI_Microcontroller.pdf),
39: [1988](https://bitsavers.trailing-edge.com/components/oki/_dataBooks/1988_OKI_Microcontroller_Data_Book.pdf).
40: 
41: ## How the dump was made
42: 
43: The MSM83C154 does not latch EA at reset, which allows the internal ROM to be
44: read:
45: 
46: 1. The AVR host loads a small dumper program (`mcs51/src/romdump.c`) at
47:    code address 0x4000, plus a stub `LJMP 0x4000` at 0x0000.
48: 2. The AVR holds EA low and releases reset. The 8052 fetches everything
49:    externally, runs the stub and jumps to the dumper.
50: 3. About 10 ms later the AVR raises EA. Code addresses 0x0000–0x3FFF now read
51:    the internal ROM. Code at 0x4000 and above is still fetched externally.
52: 4. The dumper copies code 0x0000–0x3FFF (MOVC) to data 0x0000–0x3FFF (MOVX).
53: 5. The AVR resets the 8052, reads the SRAM back and prints it over serial.
54:    `scripts/capture_romdump.py` captures the output and writes `romdump.bin`.
55: 
56: Build: `pio run -e mcs51 -t upload` (see `platformio.ini` and `README.md`).
57: 
58: ## Overview
59: 
60: | Item | Value |
61: |---|---|
62: | Reset vector | 0x0000 → 0x10E8 |
63: | INT0 vector | 0x0003 → 0x0030 |
64: | Timer 1 / Timer 2 vectors | 0x001B / 0x002B → 0x0637 |
65: | ROM checksum | 0x0000–0x3FFC, compared with 0x3FFE–0x3FFF (`B9 45`) |
66: | Config byte | 0x3FFD |
67: | ASCII strings | None |
68: | Code reached by recursive disassembly | 12,685 of 16,384 bytes |
69: | Unused | 0x36CA–0x3FFD (zero-filled) |
70: 
71: The 8052's hardware UART is not used.
72: 
73: ## Revised picture
74: 
75: The 8052 is an I/O controller sitting under a larger host computer. It has
76: three interfaces.
77: 
78: ### 1. Host mailbox (external registers F8h–FFh)
79: 
80: - **Status reads.** The host writes an internal-RAM address to FAh. Firmware
81:   returns that byte at F8h and echoes the address at F9h. Flag bytes 20h–25h
82:   and 2Eh clear when read (21h is masked with C1h), so they are host-visible
83:   error and status registers. Handler: 0x05A4.
84: - **Start command.** The host writes 01h to FDh. Firmware builds per-channel
85:   masks from each channel's state at 3Fh+n and returns status byte 21h at FDh.
86:   Handler: 0x05F1.
87: - **Debug monitor** (0x35A7–0x36C1):
88:   - Entry: host writes FCh to FBh. Firmware answers FCh at FAh and sets flag
89:     2Ah.1.
90:   - Exit: host writes FAh.
91:   - Command 8xh writes and Axh reads. Bits 0–3 pick the target:
92: 
93:     | Bit | Target |
94:     |---|---|
95:     | 0 | Internal RAM (`@R0`) |
96:     | 1 | External RAM (`MOVX @R0`) |
97:     | 2 | Link controller register (`MOVX @DPTR`, DPH = 00h) |
98:     | 3 | Port: P1, P2 or P3 (address < 2, = 2, > 2) |
99: 
100:   - Address comes from FFh and data from FEh. Read results go to FAh. The
101:     address and data are echoed to E4h/E5h.
102:   - In debug mode the main poll keeps polling channels and kicking the
103:     watchdog but never returns to the background loop, so the self-test is
104:     suspended. Status reporting and the P3.5 health output also stop.
105: - **Health output (P3.5):** outside debug mode, every 100 passes of the main
106:   poll (0x1751), status byte 21h is sent to FDh and P3.5 is updated: low when
107:   26h, 28h or 29h are non-zero, toggling while error flags 21h.1 or 21h.2 are
108:   set, otherwise high.
109: 
110: INT0 dispatch (0x0030) reads status register D9h. Bit 0 → channel receive.
111: Bit 1 → host mailbox dispatch at 0x00B2, which branches on status register
112: DFh: bit 4 → channel command (from FCh, 0x00DA), bit 2 → status read,
113: bit 3 → debug monitor, bit 5 → start command, bits 6 and 7 → writes to
114: E4h/E5h.
115: 
116: ### 2. Eight channels (external registers E0h–EFh, F0h–F7h)
117: 
118: - A command byte arrives per channel at F0h+n: 7 bits plus odd parity,
119:   delivered via INT0. It is stored in internal RAM at 37h+n.
120: - Two readings per channel at E0h+2n and E1h+2n: 7 bits plus odd parity. Both
121:   are read twice in a row (`MOVX A,@R1` twice).
122: - Each accepted command flips that channel's bit in 77h, which is written to
123:   FBh. Commands 15h and 16h don't flip it. Function not proven: handshake
124:   line or indicator.
125: - Per-channel state for the main loop's state machine is at 2Fh+n (initial
126:   state 45h). A per-channel status code is at 3Fh+n: set to values 01h–13h
127:   and compared, never counted down. Further per-channel bytes are at 48h+,
128:   50h+, 58h+, 60h+ and 68h+ (n−1).
129: 
130: ### 3. Link controller chip (DPTR 0000h–000Ah)
131: 
132: Part number unknown.
133: 
134: - Reset pulse comes from P3.3.
135: - Two ways in: direct registers, plus an indirect register file.
136: 
137: | Register | Use |
138: |---|---|
139: | 1 | Status. Bit 4 = ready for a new message. Polled up to 100 times after command 04h (0x0584). |
140: | 2 | Write: indirect register number; bit 3 set = select for reading. Read: bit 7 = ready for an indirect access (polled up to 200 times, 0x2F41). |
141: | 3 | Command. 04h = prepare to send, 01h = send, 08h = other. |
142: | 7 | Indirect data port. |
143: | 8 | Message FIFO (data in and out). |
144: | 0Ah | Destination: 30h+n, or n. |
145: 
146: - **Indirect write:** data to reg 7, then the register number to reg 2.
147:   Register numbers used: 10h–17h (per channel, 0x2F41), 80h–87h, A0h–A7h,
148:   C2h–C4h.
149: - **Indirect read:** the register number with bit 3 set to reg 2, then read
150:   reg 7.
151: - **Setup (0x08BC):**
152:   - Config C2h←28h, C3h←01h, C4h←37h.
153:   - Table 80h–87h ← 81h–88h.
154:   - Table A0h–A7h ← 97h, 80h–86h.
155:   - Every value is read back. Any mismatch goes to the 0x0CBE error path.
156: - **Sending:** command 04h and wait for ready, write bytes into the FIFO at
157:   reg 8, write the destination to reg 0Ah, then command 01h to reg 3.
158: - Link timeouts (no ready signal) set error flags 21h.2 and 24h.3.
159: - There is a loopback test that fills the FIFO with 55h/AAh and reads it back
160:   (0x0DA8–0x0DEF).
161: 
162: Writes to external register E3h appear 35 times, between steps of long
163: operations. They are most likely watchdog kicks.
164: 
165: ## Message types
166: 
167: First byte of each message sent through the link controller:
168: 
169: | First byte | Data bytes | Notes |
170: |---|---|---|
171: | 03/43, 0B/4B, 13/53, 18/58, 23/63, 2B/6B | varies | Pairs differ only in bit 6 |
172: | 06, 26, 66 | 2, 2, 0 | Variants differ in bits 5–6 |
173: | 27 | 1 | |
174: | 30 | 4 | Channel readings (see below) |
175: 
176: Startup handshake (0x0BC2), per channel:
177: 1. Indirect write C0h to register 10h+(n−1).
178: 2. Send `26 04 88` to 30h+n−1.
179: 3. Send `66` to n−1, and expect `66 04 88` back. The value written in step 2
180:    is read back.
181: 4. Send `30 11 2B 11 2B` (readings invalid) to 30h+n−1.
182: 
183: ## Command 2xh: read the channel
184: 
185: - Bits 4–6 = 010 means a data request (`(cmd & 70h) == 20h`).
186: - The reply has five bytes, built at 0x0F7C:
187: 
188:   ```
189:   30 | value(E1h+2n) hi lo | value(E0h+2n) hi lo
190:   ```
191: 
192:   It goes to destination 30h+n.
193: - A parity failure puts `11 2B` in place of that value.
194: - Each 7-bit reading goes through a lookup table: 128 entries of 2 bytes,
195:   held in 4 tables at 0x31A7, 0x32A7, 0x33A7 and 0x34A7.
196: - The tables join into one monotonic curve of about 360 entries. 0x31A7 and
197:   0x32A7 are contiguous. 0x33A7 starts 110 entries before 0x31A7's first
198:   entry, and 0x34A7 starts 18 entries after it.
199: - Command bits 0 and 1 choose the starting offset: bit 0 picks −110 (0x33A7)
200:   or +18 (0x34A7) for the first reading (E1h+2n), bit 1 picks 0 (0x31A7) or
201:   +128 (0x32A7) for the second (E0h+2n). In effect each bit selects one of two
202:   ranges.
203: - Entries 251–255 hold a sentinel value, `17 0B` (out of range).
204: - So the controller converts raw 7-bit samples into a calibrated quantity
205:   before forwarding them. That points to sensor or control values, not text.
206: 
207: ## Encoding of the table values: logarithmic, decimal floating point
208: 
209: ### The curve is logarithmic: 60 entries per decade
210: 
211: Comparing each entry with the one N entries further along, and counting exact
212: matches where only byte 0's low nibble differs (by 1):
213: 
214: | N | Exact matches |
215: |---|---|
216: | 58 | 0 |
217: | 59 | 0 |
218: | **60** | **70** |
219: | 61 | 3 |
220: | 62 | 0 |
221: 
222: - **Byte 0's low nibble is a decimal exponent.** It drops by 1 every 60
223:   entries while everything else stays the same: `2405 → 2305 → 2205`,
224:   `14AB → 13AB`, `D303 → D203`.
225: - **The mismatches are small and in the low digits.** That fits each decade
226:   being calculated separately and rounded.
227: - **Precision runs out at the bottom.** Once the exponent reaches 0 it can't
228:   drop further, so the values decay to small integers and then to `00 00`.
229:   That explains the plateaus at the end of the curve.
230: - **The values are decimal floating point:** a mantissa of about 3 digits, in
231:   an unusual nibble encoding, times 10 to the exponent. The value falls by a
232:   factor of 10 every 60 input counts.
233: - **Range:** the curve spans about 360 entries, so about 6 decades. One 7-bit
234:   reading covers about 2.1 decades. The two command bits move that window
235:   within the 6 decades.
236: 
237: So each raw reading is on a log scale, and the firmware turns it into an
238: engineering value of the form mantissa × 10ⁿ. In audio or RF terms, 60 counts
239: per decade is ⅓ dB per count for amplitude, or ⅙ dB per count for power.
240: 
241: ### Mantissa digits: unresolved
242: 
243: - The low nibble of byte 0 takes only the values 0–4 and steps down along the
244:   curve: the exponent, above.
245: - The high nibble of byte 0 counts cleanly if each nibble is decoded as
246:   `x ≥ 8 ? x − 8 : 15 − x`. That gives the order 8, 9, A–F, 7, 6 … 0. Only 13
247:   small glitches remain, at boundaries.
248: - Byte 1 reverses direction depending on its own low nibble, which looks like
249:   a reflected code.
250: - 8 decodings tested, none monotonic:
251:   - plain binary under all 8-bit permutations;
252:   - Gray code under all bit orders and XOR masks;
253:   - signed-digit forms;
254:   - reflected mixed-radix forms.
255: 
256:   The best still had 46 out-of-order steps.
257: - With the exponent identified, only the 3 mantissa nibbles remain. If they
258:   decode to familiar values, the units may become obvious.
259: 
260: ## Other tables
261: 
262: | Address | Contents |
263: |---|---|
264: | 0x308F | 256-byte bit-reverse table |
265: | 0x318E | Channel bit masks: `FF 01 02 04 08 10 20 40 80` (indexed 0–8) |
266: | 0x3196 | Inverted channel masks: `80 FE FD FB F7 EF DF BF 7F` |
267: | 0x36C2 | Inverted bit masks: `FE FD FB F7 EF DF BF 7F` |
268: | 0x1791 | Jump table of 35 `LJMP`s: per-channel state machine (dispatcher at 0x178D, `JMP @A+DPTR` at 0x1790). The state value is the byte offset into the table, so state = 3 × entry. States 4Eh–5Dh all go to 0x2CEC. |
269: 
270: ## Other routines
271: 
272: - **Startup (0x10E8):** clears external registers FCh and FBh, sets SP = DFh.
273:   Init at 0x0654 reads the reset cause and records it in status byte 20h for
274:   the host: IRQ_STATUS (D9h) bit 2 → 08h, bit 3 → 04h, HOST_STATUS (DFh)
275:   bit 1 → 02h. IRQ_STATUS bit 4 reinitialises only the link and channels.
276:   Then it clears internal RAM, checksums the whole ROM (0x07E1), tests
277:   internal RAM, configures the link controller and starts Timer 2 and INT0.
278: - **Background self-test (0x1117):** between passes of the main poll, a
279:   rolling self-test runs:
280:   1. ROM checksum, 20 bytes per step.
281:   2. R0/R1 test.
282:   3. Internal RAM write/read test (FFh, 00h), 16 bytes per step.
283:   4. Internal RAM 80h–DFh checksum, compared with the first pass.
284:   5. Link controller config read-back.
285:   6. Link loopback test (0x13F3).
286:   7. Stack sentinel: internal RAM FFh must still be FFh.
287: 
288:   Failures set error bits in status bytes 21h, 22h and 24h for the host.
289:   Config byte bit 2 (flag 2Ah.7) skips the self-test entirely.
290: - **Per-channel records:** upper internal RAM 80h–DFh holds 8 records of 12
291:   bytes, one per channel (80h + 12(n−1)).
292: - **Timer ISR (0x0637):** Timer 2 with RCAP2 = FE80h (384 machine cycles per
293:   tick). Drives decimal counters at 10h–13h: every tick, 10, 100 and 1000
294:   ticks.
295: - **Per-channel input lines:** P1 is read while P3.1 (0x2DD2) or P3.0+P3.1
296:   (0x2DE4) is pulsed, then masked with the channel's bit. Two banks of 8
297:   per-channel inputs: switches or presence lines.
298: 
299: ## Suspected firmware bug
300: 
301: In the state 45h handler, at 0x2C5C, the code computes `FFh + R7` (= n−1)
302: and writes 10h through it. That lands in internal RAM 00h–07h, the bank 0
303: registers, instead of the per-channel status code at 3Fh+n that the
304: equivalent code at 0x0788 uses. For channel 8 it overwrites R7, the channel
305: loop counter. It only runs on one path (command 07h received while the
306: channel is not faulty), which may be why it went unnoticed.
307: 
308: ## Corrections to earlier claims
309: 
310: - The message first bytes are types that come in variants (see table above).
311:   Calling this "3-bit type + 4-bit code" was wrong.
312: - Commands 15h and 16h are not discarded. They are processed but don't flip
313:   the channel bit.
314: - The F0h–F7h command bytes use odd parity, not even. The check is
315:   `JNB P`: an even number of 1 bits is an error.
316: - Link register 2's bit 7 means "ready for an indirect access", not "data
317:   available". Bit 7 of a value written to reg 2 is part of the register
318:   number, not a write strobe.
319: - 3Fh+n holds a per-channel status code, not a timeout counter.
320: - Host mailbox dispatch bits were misassigned: DFh bit 4 is the channel
321:   command, bit 2 the status read.
322: - The P3.5 health output is not driven in debug mode. It is driven in
323:   normal operation. 0x2F41 waits for it, then writes R3 to indirect register
324:   10h+(n−1).
325: - The constants 01h, 02h and 04h in comparisons are mostly compared against
326:   per-channel state variables, not received characters. They are not
327:   evidence of ASCII control characters (STX/EOT).
328: 
329: ## Assessment
330: 
331: The firmware converts 8 channels of 7-bit log-scale readings into decimal
332: floating-point values and sends them as addressed messages. It is set up by,
333: and reports status to, a host processor, which has full peek/poke debug
334: access. It is a data-acquisition front end. Text-serial is ruled out.
335: Music/MIDI is unlikely: there are no MIDI status bytes and the data has parity.
336: 
337: ### What the design implies
338: 
339: | Feature | Implication |
340: |---|---|
341: | Six-decade log scale, decimal floating-point output | A physical quantity measured across decades |
342: | Two readings per channel, on different parts of the curve | Two related measurements, or two detectors/ranges per head |
343: | Sentinel for out of range, `11 2B` for "invalid" | The receiver displays or logs these values |
344: | Per channel: command byte, two readings, a configuration block with checksum, six device types | Smart remote sensor heads, not bare analog inputs |
345: | 7-bit odd parity everywhere, NAK (15h) and SYN (16h) handled specially | The heads talk to the board over ASCII-style asynchronous serial links |
346: | ROM checksum, RAM tests, watchdog, stack check, reset cause reported to the host | Built for high reliability. Unusual for consumer equipment |
347: | Host peek/poke debug monitor | Intelligent I/O card under a supervisory CPU, serviced in the field |
348: | Mask ROM, customer part number | Made in volume for one company's product |
349: 
350: ### Hypotheses, most likely first
351: 
352: 1. **Multi-channel monitoring concentrator for log-range instruments.**
353:    Candidates: radiation monitoring (dose-rate and count-rate meters commonly
354:    span 6 decades on a log scale), vacuum gauges (ion and Pirani gauges have
355:    log outputs spanning decades), or gas detection. Fits the heavy
356:    self-testing, the reset-cause reporting and decimal values for display.
357:    The two readings per channel would suit dose rate plus integrated dose, or
358:    two detector ranges.
359: 2. **Audio or RF level system.** 60 counts per decade suits dB-to-linear
360:    conversion, and 8 channels is typical of a console or metering system.
361:    Against it: decimal floating point is an odd choice for gain coefficients,
362:    and the self-test effort seems more than a mixer would carry.
363: 3. **Building or process control** (temperatures, setpoints). Least likely:
364:    those quantities don't span decades.
365: 
366: Confidence is moderate on the overall architecture and low on the specific
367: application.
368: 
369: ### What would narrow it down
370: 
371: 1. Original tubes or reels, labels, other parts with a `79X` prefix, or boards
372:    these chips came from.
373: 2. Other chips in the same batch with a different `79Xnnnn` or `-nn` marking,
374:    meaning other ROM programs from the same maker.
375: 3. The makerspace donor, who might know the employer or equipment.
376: 4. OKI's data books, for the marking and date-code layout.
377: 5. Decoding the mantissa nibbles.
378: 
379: Every register role in this document is inferred from how the code uses it.
380: The chips on the original board would settle most open questions, the link
381: controller's part number above all.
382: 
383: ## Tools
384: 
385: - `romdump_annotated.lst`: annotated disassembly, generated by
386:   `python3 tools/annotate.py`. Names and comments come from
387:   `tools/romdump_annotations.py`. Register accesses, per-channel array
388:   pointers, channel mask lookups and state assignments are annotated
389:   automatically. Each state handler gets a summary of the states it sets and
390:   the routines it calls.
391: - `tools/dis51.py`: a minimal recursive-descent 8051 disassembler. Extra entry
392:   points (hex) follow the ROM path. To include the 0x1791 jump table and the
393:   0x00CB mailbox jump table:
394: 
395:   ```
396:   python3 tools/dis51.py romdump.bin 35A7 05A4 05E5 05F1 05EB 062E \
397:     $(python3 -c "print(' '.join(f'{0x1791+3*i:04X}' for i in range(35)))") \
398:     > rom.lst
399:   ```

1: # MSM83C154 ROM Dump
2: 
3: A dump and analysis of the 16 KB internal mask ROM of an OKI MSM83C154
4: (8051-family) microcontroller, found among the pile of MCS-51 parts in my
5: [makerspace](https://ashevillemakers.org/)'s electronics supply drawers.
6: 
7: The chips turned out to be preprogrammed. This repository contains the tooling
8: used to read the ROM out, the dump itself, and an analysis of what the program
9: does.
10: 
11: It is a branch of my 8052 LED sign project, which provided the hardware: an
12: 8052 running from SRAM that an ATmega328 loads on its behalf. I'm documenting
13: that project on my blog,
14: https://www.blog.montgomerie.net/tags/makerspace-mcu-series/.
15: 
16: 
17: ## Contents
18: 
19: | Path | What |
20: |---|---|
21: | `romdump.bin` | The 16,384-byte ROM dump. Its internal checksum verifies. |
22: | `ROM_ANALYSIS.md` | What the program does. |
23: | `romdump_annotated.lst` | Annotated disassembly. |
24: | `tools/dis51.py` | Minimal recursive-descent 8051 disassembler used for the analysis. |
25: | `tools/annotate.py`, `tools/romdump_annotations.py` | Generator and annotation data for the annotated disassembly. |
26: | `mcs51/src/romdump.c` | Dumper, run by the 8052. |
27: | `avr_host/src/` | AVR host: loads the dumper, runs it, prints the dump over serial. |
28: | `scripts/capture_romdump.py` | Captures the serial output into `romdump.bin`. |
29: | `hardware/` | KiCad schematic and PCB of the circuit. |
30: | `docs/RAM:ROM Shadowing.txt` | Notes on the SRAM address decode the dumper relies on. |
31: 
32: 
33: ## How the dump works
34: 
35: The MSM83C154 does not latch its EA (External Access) pin at reset, so the
36: internal ROM can be switched on after the chip has started running external
37: code:
38: 
39: 1. The AVR writes the dumper to SRAM at code address 0x4000, and a stub
40:    `LJMP 0x4000` at 0x0000.
41: 2. With EA held low, the AVR releases the 8052's reset. The 8052 runs the stub
42:    from external memory and jumps to the dumper.
43: 3. The AVR raises EA. Code addresses 0x0000–0x3FFF now read the internal ROM.
44:    Code at 0x4000 and above is still fetched externally.
45: 4. The dumper copies code 0x0000–0x3FFF (MOVC) to data 0x0000–0x3FFF (MOVX).
46: 5. The AVR puts the 8052 back into reset, reads the SRAM, and prints it.
47: 
48: The 8052's EA pin must be wired to AVR pin PD2.
49: 
50: 
51: ## Running it
52: 
53: This is built with [PlatformIO](https://platformio.org). On Apple Silicon Macs,
54: PlatformIO's MCS-51 and AVR toolchains need Rosetta.
55: 
56: ```
57: pio run -e mcs51 -t upload
58: ~/.platformio/penv/bin/python scripts/capture_romdump.py [port] [output.bin]
59: ```
60: 
61: Uploading the `mcs51` environment builds the dumper, then builds and uploads
62: the AVR host with the dumper compiled into it. The capture script resets the
63: AVR, so the whole sequence (RAM test, load, dump) runs again while it listens.
64: The serial monitor runs at 38400 baud.
65: 
66:

21: def dname(a):
22:     if a in SFR: return SFR[a]
23:     if a in IRAM_NAMES: return IRAM_NAMES[a]

110: VECTORS = [0x0000, 0x0003, 0x000B, 0x0013, 0x001B, 0x0023, 0x002B]
111: 
112: def trace(rom, extra):
113:     """Recursive-descent trace from the vectors plus `extra` entry points.
114:     Returns (code, labels, xrefs, ijmps): code maps address ->
115:     (length, text, targets, kind)."""
116:     entries = VECTORS + list(extra)
117:     code = {}            # addr -> (len, text, targets, kind)
118:     labels = collections.defaultdict(set)   # addr -> {'call','jmp',...}
119:     xrefs = collections.defaultdict(set)
120:     ijmps = []
121:     work = list(entries)
122:     for e in entries: labels[e].add('entry')
123:     while work:
124:         pc = work.pop()
125:         while 0 <= pc < len(rom) and pc not in code:
126:             n, t, tg, kind = decode(rom, pc)
127:             code[pc] = (n, t, tg, kind)
128:             for x in tg:
129:                 labels[x].add(kind or 'jmp'); xrefs[x].add(pc)
130:                 if x < len(rom): work.append(x)
131:             if kind == 'ijmp': ijmps.append(pc)
132:             if kind in ('jmp', 'ret', 'ijmp'): break
133:             pc += n
134:     return code, labels, xrefs, ijmps
135: 
136: def main():
137:     rom = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read()
138:     extra = [int(x, 16) for x in sys.argv[2:]]
139:     code, labels, xrefs, ijmps = trace(rom, extra)
140:     covered = set()
141:     for a, (n, *_rest) in code.items(): covered.update(range(a, a+n))
142:     out = []
143:     a = 0
144:     while a < len(rom):
145:         if a in code:
146:             n, t, tg, kind = code[a]
147:             if a in labels:
148:                 kinds = ','.join(sorted(labels[a]))
149:                 xs = ' '.join(f'{x:04X}' for x in sorted(xrefs[a])[:8])
150:                 out.append(f'\nL{a:04X}:  ; [{kinds}] from {xs}')
151:             hexb = ' '.join(f'{rom[a+i]:02X}' for i in range(n))
152:             out.append(f'  {a:04X}  {hexb:<9} {t}')
153:             a += n
154:         else:
155:             start = a
156:             while a < len(rom) and a not in code: a += 1
157:             chunk = rom[start:a]
158:             out.append(f'  {start:04X}  ; --- {a-start} bytes not reached as code ---')
159:             for i in range(0, min(len(chunk), 64), 16):
160:                 out.append(f'  {start+i:04X}  DB ' + ' '.join(f'{b:02X}' for b in chunk[i:i+16]))
161:             if len(chunk) > 64: out.append('        ...')
162:     print('\n'.join(out))
163:     print(f'\n; {len(covered)} of {len(rom)} bytes reached as code. '
164:           f'{sum(1 for l in labels.values() if "call" in l)} called routines. '
165:           f'Indirect jumps (JMP @A+DPTR) at: {" ".join(f"{x:04X}" for x in ijmps)}', file=sys.stderr)
166: 
167: if __name__ == "__main__":
168:     main()

293: Configure channel R7. Only in states 4Eh-5Dh, otherwise a protocol error.

297: at WIN_E9. The second reads the block back, and the reply must match the

313: 0x0637: """\
314: Timer 2 tick (reload FE80h = 384 machine cycles). Decimal counters:

318: 0x0654: """\
319: Initialisation. Reads the reset cause and records it in STAT20/STAT21 for

322:   IRQ_STATUS b4 -> reinitialise the link and channels only.

326: 
327: 0x07E1: """\
328: Checksum 0000h-3FFCh: 16-bit sum, compared with 3FFEh (low) and 3FFFh

331: 0x0822: """\
332: iRAM test: each byte 01h-FFh is saved, written DAh and 25h, read back and

334: 
335: 0x08BC: """\
336: Link controller setup. Pulse P3.3 to reset it, then write its indirect
337: registers: config C2h=28h, C4h=37h, table 80h-87h = 81h-88h,
338: table A0h-A7h = 97h, 80h-86h, C3h=01h. Every value is read back. Any
339: mismatch goes to link_error.""",

341: 0x0BC2: """\
342: Per-channel handshake. For each channel, an indirect write 10h+n-1 = C0h.
343: Then for each channel: send 26 04 88 to 30h+n-1, send 66 to n-1 and expect
344: 66 04 88 back (the value just written), then send 30 11 2B 11 2B (readings
345: invalid) to 30h+n-1.""",
346: 
347: 0x0F7C: """\
348: Send channel R7's two readings. Message: 30, then two bytes for the reading
349: at WIN_E1+2(n-1), then two for WIN_E0+2(n-1), to destination 30h+n-1.
350: Each reading is 7 bits + odd parity, looked up in the conversion curve.
351: R5 bit 0 picks the range for the first, bit 1 for the second. A parity error
352: sends 11 2B instead.
353: The curve is logarithmic, 60 entries per decade, giving decimal floating
354: point: byte 0's low nibble is the exponent, the other 3 nibbles the mantissa.""",
355: 
356: 0x10E8: """\
357: Reset entry. Clear REG_FC and CH_TOGGLE, set the stack, initialise, read the

360: 0x1117: """\
361: Background loop. Runs the main poll between steps of a rolling self-test:
362:   1. ROM checksum, 20 bytes per step.
363:   2. R0/R1 test.
364:   3. iRAM write/read test (FFh, 00h), 16 bytes per step.
365:   4. iRAM 80h-DFh checksum, compared with the first pass.
366:   5. Link controller config read-back.
367:   6. Link loopback test.
368:   7. Stack sentinel: iRAM FFh must still be FFh.
369: Each failure sets error bits for the host.""",
370: 
371: 0x1679: """\
372: Main poll. One pass: for each channel 8..1, if there is a command, a data
373: request (2xh) is answered immediately with send_readings, anything else
374: goes to the channel's state handler with R5 = command. A handler accepts the
375: command by clearing R5; a byte that arrived meanwhile is then fetched from
376: CHn_CMD. With no command, the handler runs with R5 = 0. Deferred data
377: requests are answered at the end of each channel's turn.
378: 
379: Passes repeat (via debug_mode_poll) and the routine only returns every 100
380: passes. In debug mode it never returns, which suspends the self-test.""",
381: 
382: 0x1751: """\
383: End of a main poll pass (also entered directly in debug mode). Kick the
384: watchdog and start another pass. Every 100 passes, unless in debug mode:
385: report STAT21 to the host, update HEALTH_OUT (low if any channel is faulty,
386: toggling while ERROR/FAULT is set, otherwise high) and return.""",
387: 
388: 0x178D: """\
389: State dispatch: the state value is a byte offset into the jump table, so
390: state = 3 x entry. R7 = channel, R5 = command byte (0 if none).""",
391: 
392: 0x2CEC: """\
393: Handler for states 4Eh, 51h, 54h, 57h, 5Ah, 5Dh (channel not yet running).

397: Debug monitor. Enter: host writes FCh to HOST_DBGCMD, we answer FCh.
398: Exit: FAh. In debug mode:
399:   8xh = write, Axh = read. Bits 0-3: iRAM, XRAM (@R0), link register,
400:   port (address < 2: P1, = 2: P2, > 2: P3).
401: Address from HOST_DBGADDR, data from HOST_DATA, reply on HOST_REPLY.
402: Address and data are echoed to ACK_E4/ACK_E5.""",

The MSM83C154/MSM80C154 is a high performance 8-bit one-chip microcontroller implementing large integration, high speed and low power consumption by 2 ,um silicon gate CMOS process technology. The MSM83C154 features 16K byte ROM, 256 byte RAM, 32 I/O ports, three 16-bit timer/counters, multifunctional serial port and clock generator. In addition, the MSM83C154 has three standby modes enabling further power reduction. The MSM80C154 is identical to the MSM83C154 except the omission of 16K byte ROM.

• 16-bit timer/counters

Output of the read strobe signal when data is read from external data memory.

ALE Address latch enable output for latching the lower 8-bit address during external memory access. Two ALE pulses are activated per machine cycle except during external data memory access at which time one ALE pulse is skipped.

PSEN Program store enable output which enable the external memory output to the bus during external program memory access. Two PSEN pulses are activated per machine cycle except during external data memory access at which two PSEN pulses are skipped.

EA When EA is held at "H"level, the MSM83C154 executes instructions from internal program memory at address OOOOH to 3FFFH, and executes instructions from external program memory above address 3FFFH. When EA is held at "L" level, the MSM80C154/MSM83C154 executes instructions from external program memory for all addresses.

The MSM80C154S/MSM83C154S covers the functions and operating range of the existing
MSM80C154/83C154/80C51F/80C31F.
The MSM80C154S is identical to the MSM83C154S except it does not contain the internal
program memory (ROM).
FEATURES
• Operating range
Operating frequency
Operating voltage
Operating temperature
: 0 to 3 MHz (Vcc=2.2 to 6.0 V)
0 to 12 MHz (Vcc=3.0 to 6.0 V)
0 to 24 MHz (Vcc=4.5 to 6.0 V)
: 2.2 to 6.0 V
: –40 to +85°C (Operation at +125°C conforms to
the other specification.)
• Fully static circuit
• Upward compatible with the MSM80C51F/80C31F
• On-chip program memory
: 16K words x 8 bits ROM (MSM83C154S only)
• On-chip data memory
: 256 words x 8 bits RAM
• External program memory address space : 64K bytes ROM (Max)
• External data memory address space
: 64K bytes RAM
• I/O ports
: 4 ports x 8 bits
(Port 1, 2, 3, impedance programmable) : 32
• 16-bit timer/counters
: 3
• Multifunctional serial port
: I/O Expansion mode
: UART mode (featuring error detection)
• 6-source 2-priority level
Interrupt and multi-level
Interrupt available by programming IP and IE registers
• Memory-mapped special function registers
• Bit addressable data memory and SFRs
• Minimum instruction cycle
: 500 ns @ 24 MHz operation
• Standby functions
: Power-down mode (oscillator stop)
Activated by software or hardware; providing
ports with floating or active status

GENERAL DESCRIPTION
The MSM80C154S/MSM83C154S, designed for the high speed version of the existing MSM80C154/MSM83C154, is a higher performance 8-bit microcontroller providing low-power consumption. The MSM80C154S/MSM83C154S covers the functions and operating range of the existing MSM80C154/83C154/80C51F/80C31F. The MSM80C154S is identical to the MSM83C154S except it does not contain the internal program memory (ROM).
FEATURES
• Operating range Operating frequency : 0 to 3 MHz (Vcc=2.2 to 6.0 V) 0 to 12 MHz (Vcc=3.0 to 6.0 V) 0 to 24 MHz (Vcc=4.5 to 6.0 V) Operating voltage : 2.2 to 6.0 V Operating temperature : –40 to +85°C (Operation at +125°C conforms to the other specification.) • Fully static circuit • Upward compatible with the MSM80C51F/80C31F • On-chip program memory : 16K words x 8 bits ROM (MSM83C154S only) • On-chip data memory : 256 words x 8 bits RAM • External program memory address space : 64K bytes ROM (Max) • External data memory address space : 64K bytes RAM • I/O ports : 4 ports x 8 bits (Port 1, 2, 3, impedance programmable) : 32 • 16-bit timer/counters : 3 • Multifunctional serial port : I/O Expansion mode : UART mode (featuring error detection) • 6-source 2-priority level Interrupt and multi-level Interrupt available by programming IP and IE registers • Memory-mapped special function registers • Bit addressable data memory and SFRs • Minimum instruction cycle : 500 ns @ 24 MHz operation • Standby functions : Power-down mode (oscillator stop) Activated by software or hardware; providing ports with floating or active status The software power-down stet mode is termi- nated by interrupt signal enabling execution from the interrupted address.

Symbol Descriptipn
Bidirectional I/O ports. They are also the data/address bus (input/output of data and output of lower 8-bit address when external memory is accessed). They are open-drain outputs when used as I/O ports, but 3-state outputs when used as data/address bus.
P1.0 to P1.7 are quasi-bidirectional I/O ports. They are pulled up internally when used as input ports. Two of them have the following secondary functions: •P1.0 (T2) •P1.1 (T2EX) : used as external clock input pins for the timer/counter 2. : used as trigger input for the timer/counter 2 to be reloaded or captured; causing the timer/counter 2 interrupt.

**GENERAL DESCRIPTION**

The MSM85C154 is a device whose built-in ROM is replaced by external EPROM using the piggy- back method. External EPROM capacity is up to 16K bytes. It can be used for evaluation of programs for MSM83C154.

MSM80C154S/83C154S ¡ Semiconductor
GENERAL DESCRIPTION
The MSM80C154S/MSM83C154S, designed for the high speed version of the existing MSM80C154/MSM83C154, is a higher performance 8-bit microcontroller providing low-power consumption. The MSM80C154S/MSM83C154S covers the functions and operating range of the existing MSM80C154/83C154/80C51F/80C31F. The MSM80C154S is identical to the MSM83C154S except it does not contain the internal program memory (ROM).
FEATURES
• Operating range Operating frequency : 0 to 3 MHz (Vcc=2.2 to 6.0 V) 0 to 12 MHz (Vcc=3.0 to 6.0 V) 0 to 24 MHz (Vcc=4.5 to 6.0 V) Operating voltage : 2.2 to 6.0 V Operating temperature : –40 to +85°C (Operation at +125°C conforms to the other specification.)

* ## MSM80C154S Product details
* GENERAL DESCRIPTION The MSM80C154S/MSM83C154S, designed for the high speed version of the existing MSM80C154/MSM83C154, is a higher performance 8-bit microcontroller providing low-power consumption. The MSM80C154S/MSM83C154S covers the functions and operating range of the existing MSM80C154/83C154/80C51F/80C31F. The MSM80C154S is identical to the MSM83C154S except it does not contain the internal program memory (ROM). FEATURES • Operating range Operating frequency : 0 to 3 MHz (Vcc=2.2 to 6.0 V) 0 to 12 MHz (Vcc =3.0 to 6.0 V) 0 to 24 MHz (Vcc =4.5 to 6.0 V) Operating voltage : 2.2 to 6.0 V Operating temperature : –40 to +85°C (Operation at +125°C conforms to the other specification.)

## [GoFast 8051 Floating-Point Library User's Guide](https://smxrtos.com/doc/ussw/gofast/gofast8051.pdf)
Published: 2010-08-17T00:00:00.000Z

GoFast® 8051 Floating-Point Library User’s Guide

August 17, 2010

1 Introduction........................................................................................................... 1 1.1 Purpose........................................................................................................ 1

1.2 Definitions................................................................................................... 2

...

The GoFast floating point library includes FPAC and DPAC parts. FPAC provides floating point functions based on the IEEE single precision floating point format. DPAC extends the FPAC functionality to the IEEE double precision floating point format.

The library consists of the basic floating point operations (ADD/SUBTRACT, MULTIPLY, DIVIDE), data conversion routines (ASCII to/from floating point, integer to/from floating point), functions (sine, cosine, tangent, arctangent, common and natural logarithm, exponentiation of e, square root, and floating point to integer power). In addition, DPAC provides precision translation routines for conversion between single and double precision formats.

...

GoFast 8051 Floating-Point Library User’s Guide

1.2 Definitions Floating point is a method of representing numeric values (integers and non-integers) in a computer. It uses three fields for this:

• The sign tells whether the number is positive or negative. • The exponent tells where the decimal point goes. • The mantissa (also called the significand) gives the digits.

To get the actual value of the number, you raise 2 to the power of the exponent and multiply this with the mantissa. (For details such as bias and scaling, see the IEEE 754 document.) In the IEEE 754 standard, single-precision numbers take up 32 bits, double-precision

numbers twice that. The useful range for singles is approximately 10 -38 to 10 38 , for doubles 10 -308 to 10 308 . The relative precision (typical rounding error in one arithmetic operation) is of the order of 10 -7 for singles, 10 -16 for doubles.

1.3 The IEEE Floating Point Format The number format on which FPAC operates is the IEEE 754 single precision standard. Its representation, in bit form is: S EEE EEEE E MMM MMMM MMMM MMMM MMMM MMMM

byte 3 byte 2 byte 1 byte 0

“S” is the sign bit (1 if negative, 0 if positive). The “E” field is the two’s exponent. It is a two’s complement value biased by 127 (decimal. The “M” field is the 23-bit normalized mantissa. The most significant bit is always assumed to be 1, and so is not explicitly stored. This yields an effective precision of 24 bits.

...

Where N is a digit, n is the fractional part with trailing zeroes suppressed, “.” is a decimal point, “#” is either “+” or “-“, and “d” is a digit in the ten’s exponent. See section 6.0 for a description of the error conditions underflow, INF, and NaN. The symbolic constant FDDIG specifies the number of digits the single precision routine will display.

...

All function results are correct to within one or two mantissa bits except for tangent near its discontiguous points and the logarithms very near 1.0 (though this is a representation problem of floating point values, not an algorithm error). See the C API is implementation in files gf_dp*.a51 and gf_fp*.a51 for example use of the assembly API. Single Double Description

FPEXP DPEXP e raised to the power

FPLN DPLN Natural logarithm

FPLOG DPLOG Common logarithm

FPSIN DPSIN Sine (note: limited domain, see 6.0)

...

## [Improved Decimal Floating-Point Logarithmic Converter Based on Selection by Rounding](https://www.computer.org/csdl/journal/tc/2012/05/ttc2012050607/13rRUxly8WS)
Published: 2012-05-01T00:00:00.000Z

4. 2012.05
IEEE Transactions on Computers

Improved Decimal Floating-Point Logarithmic Converter Based on Selection by Rounding May 2012, pp. 607-621, vol. 61

DOI Bookmark: 10.1109/TC.2011.43

Authors

Dongdong Chen , University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon Liu Han , University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon Younhee Choi , University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon Seok-Bum Ko , University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon
Download PDF SHARE ARTICLE
Generate Citation

Keywords

Decimal Floating Point, Decimal Logarithmic Converter, Digit Recurrence Algorithm, Selection By Rounding

Abstract

This paper presents the algorithm and architecture of the decimal floating-point (DFP) logarithmic converter, based on the digit-recurrence algorithm with selection by rounding. The proposed approach can compute faithful DFP logarithm results for any one of the three DFP formats specified in the IEEE 754-2008 standard.

**GENERAL DESCRIPTION**

The MSM85C154 is a device whose built-in ROM is replaced by external EPROM using the piggy- back method. External EPROM capacity is up to 16K bytes. It can be used for evaluation of programs for MSM83C154.

MSM80C154S/83C154S ¡ Semiconductor
GENERAL DESCRIPTION
The MSM80C154S/MSM83C154S, designed for the high speed version of the existing MSM80C154/MSM83C154, is a higher performance 8-bit microcontroller providing low-power consumption. The MSM80C154S/MSM83C154S covers the functions and operating range of the existing MSM80C154/83C154/80C51F/80C31F. The MSM80C154S is identical to the MSM83C154S except it does not contain the internal program memory (ROM).
FEATURES
• Operating range Operating frequency : 0 to 3 MHz (Vcc=2.2 to 6.0 V) 0 to 12 MHz (Vcc=3.0 to 6.0 V) 0 to 24 MHz (Vcc=4.5 to 6.0 V) Operating voltage : 2.2 to 6.0 V Operating temperature : –40 to +85°C (Operation at +125°C conforms to the other specification.)

But the equivalent at 0x0788 sets MSG_FLAGS=88h, clears 2Ch, sets 28h, state4E, code[n]=10h, CH_ACTIVE, 21h.7. The 2C5C path writes code[n] then sets CH_ACTIVE, state 4E, clears 1Ch, iwrite C0, sets 28h... So yes it's a duplicate path but bug. Wait at 2C5C A=FFh + R7 = R7-1 (0..7) and writes 10h to internal RAM location n-1. For n=8 writes address 7 = R7 (bank 0), clobbers loop counter? But at this point R7 is channel number in current handler, not loop counter? Need see how main loop iterates. It might indeed clobber R7 if R7=8, causing loop issues. But perhaps R7 is saved? Let's check main_poll. Anyway plausible.

; Initialisation. Reads the reset cause and records it in STAT20/STAT21 for
; the host:
;   IRQ_STATUS b2 -> 08h   IRQ_STATUS b3 -> 04h   HOST_STATUS b1 -> 02h
;   IRQ_STATUS b4 -> reinitialise the link and channels only.
; Then clears iRAM (keeping the reset cause), sets up the host registers,
; checksums the ROM, tests iRAM, configures the link controller and starts
; Timer 2 and INT0.
;   Sets state: 45h
;   Calls: link_init, channel_handshake, rom_checksum_full, L0768

## Assistant

_Thinking:_

Timer ISR confirmed. But doc says "Drives decimal counters at 10h–13h: every tick, 10, 100 and 1000 ticks." Correct. Note DIV_10 initialized to 0Ah at init, so first increment at 10 ticks. Fine.

However, Timer 2 RCAP2=FE80 => 384 machine cycles per tick. At 12 MHz, 384 cycles = 384 µs (1 µs machine cycle) = 2.604 kHz. At 11.0592 MHz = 384*1.085 µs = 416.6 µs. So tick ~2.4 kHz. Maybe counters are milliseconds? 384 cycles at 12 MHz = 0.384 ms. Not exact. Could be **timer for timeouts**, not necessarily decimal counters. The doc says "decimal counters" because they count by 10. Fine.

## Assistant

_Thinking:_

Init: interesting reset cause mapping. Doc says "IRQ_STATUS (D9h) bit 2 → 08h, bit 3 → 04h, HOST_STATUS (DFh) bit 1 → 02h. IRQ_STATUS bit 4 reinitialises only the link and channels." Code: if D9 bit2 -> STAT20=08, STAT21=08; bit3 -> STAT20=04, STAT21=08; DF bit1 -> STAT20=02, STAT21=08; D9 bit4 -> STAT20=00, STAT21 bit3, 20h bit5, 21h bit0, etc. So yes. But the fallthrough order: bit2 checked before bit3 before host bit1 before bit4. If multiple bits set, priority. Fine.

At 0x06FE, it saves STAT20/STAT21 into TL1/TH1 (weird use of SFR as scratch), saves E0/E1 into TL0/TH0, clears 01h-FFh, then restores. The annotation says iRAM E0/E1 preserved across the clear. Why E0/E1? Because `MOV R0,#E0h` etc. Actually it saves iRAM E0h and E1h. Fine. But note it clears 00h? Loop: R0=0; DEC R0 -> FF; writes @R0=0; CJNE R0,#0 loops; so clears FF..01, leaves 00. Good.

Then it writes F8h-FBh to 0. Sets 20h/21h from scratch. Restores E0/E1. Writes A7h to external FF (host). Checks config byte at 3FFD: if nonzero -> A=0x81 else 0x01, writes to FE. Config bit1/2 set later in start. So any nonzero config byte → 81h at FE. Doc says "Config byte bit 1 -> CFG_BIT1, bit2 -> CFG_BIT2, nonzero -> 81h replies". Correct in annotation; main doc "Config byte | 0x3FFD" but no detail. However doc says "Config byte bit 2 (flag 2Ah.7) skips self-test entirely." Actually code checks bit2 (04h) → CFG_BIT2, and background loop `JB CFG_BIT2,background_loop` skips self-test. Correct. Bit1 (02h) → CFG_BIT1, used where? Search.

; Debug monitor. Enter: host writes FCh to HOST_DBGCMD, we answer FCh.
; Exit: FAh. In debug mode:
;   8xh = write, Axh = read. Bits 0-3: iRAM, XRAM (@R0), link register,
;   port (address < 2: P1, = 2: P2, > 2: P3).
; Address from HOST_DBGADDR, data from HOST_DATA, reply on HOST_REPLY.
; Address and data are echoed to ACK_E4/ACK_E5.

## [8051 Microcontrollers Hardware Manual - Microchip Technology](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/aemDocuments/documents/OTH/ProductDocuments/UserGuides/doc4316.pdf)
Published: 2007-01-22T00:00:00.000Z

The 8051 instruction set is optimized for 8-bit control applications. It provides a variety of fast addressing modes for accessing the internal RAM to facilitate byte operations on small data structures. The instruction set provides extensive support for one-bit vari- ables as a separate data type, allowing direct bit manipulation in control and logic systems that require Boolean processing.
An overview of the 8051 instruction set is presented below, with a brief description of how certain instructions might be used.
1.1 Program Status Word The Program Status Word (PSW) contains several status bits that reflect the current state of the CPU. The PSW, shown in Table 1-1 on page 3, resides in SFR space. It contains the Carry bit, the Auxiliary Carry (for BCD operations), the two register bank select bits, the Overflow flag, a parity bit, and two user-definable status flags.
The Carry bit, other than serving the functions of a Carry bit in arithmetic operations, also serves as the “Accumulator” for a number of Boolean operations.
The bits RS0 and RS1 are used to select one of the four register banks shown below.
A number of instructions refer to these RAM locations as R0 through R7. The selection of which of the four banks is being referred to is made on the basis of the bits RS0 and RS1 at execution time.
The parity bit reflects the number of 1’s in the Accumulator: P = 1 if the Accumulator contains an odd number of 1’s, and P = 0 if the Accumulator contains an even number of 1’s. Thus the number of 1’s in the Accumulator plus P is always even.
Two bits in the PSW are uncommitted and may be used as general purpose status flags.
The PSW register contains program status information as detailed in Table 1-1.

## [8051 - SEGGER Knowledge Base](https://kb.segger.com/8051)

8051

From SEGGER Knowledge Base
Jump to navigation Jump to search
8051 is a term for Intel's MCS-51 single chip microcontroller (MCU). It was one of the first microcontrollers ever. The instruction set is still in use in a lot of modern designs.

Contents

* 1 Speed
* 2 Memory architecture
* 2.1 Internal RAM (IRAM)
* 2.2 Special fuction registers
* 2.3 XRAM

...

Internal RAM can be adressed with an 8-bit architecture (@R0, @R1, or immediate-8), meaning that up to 256 bits of RAM is possible. Not a whole lot by today's standards. In addition to that, only the @R0 and @R1 address modes can actually access the entire IRAM. For direct access (address is the second byte of the instruction), only the lower half from 0x00 to 0x7F can be accessed. If bit 7 of an address is set, the SFRs are accessed instead.

Special fuction registers

The special function registers(SFRs) overlap the IRAM's address space. Direct accesses to the upper half (0x80-0xFF) access the SFRs instead of the IRAM. Indirect read or write operations (using @R0 or @R1) access IRAM.

...

Program Memory (PMEM)

Registers

The classic 8051 has the following registers:
* PC—16-bit program counter. Contains the address for the place it should readg the next instruction
* A—Accumulator. 8-bit register used by most instructions. Memory mapped to 0xE0
* B–8-bit registers are used as extension to A for multiply and divide. Memory mapped to 0xF0
* SP–8-bit stack pointer
* DP–Data pointer. 16-bit register used by instructions accessing PMEM and XRAM. Memory mapped to 0x82-83
* PSW-Program status word. 8-bit register that contains various flags
* R0-R7-4 banks of 8 8-bit general purpose registers. Memory mapped to 0x0-0x1f, where the first bank uses the first 8 B from 0..7. The selected bank is chosen by the 2 RSB bits in the PSW.

1.2 Addressing Modes

The addressing modes in the 8051 instruction set are as follows:
1.2.1 Direct Addressing In direct addressing the operand is specified by an 8-bit address field in the instruction. Only 128 Lowest bytes of internal Data RAM and SFRs can be directly addressed.
1.2.2 Indirect Addressing In indirect addressing the instruction specifies a register which contains the address of the operand. Both internal and external RAM can be indirectly addressed.
The address register for 8-bit addresses can be R0 or R1 of the selected register bank, or the Stack Pointer. The address register for 16-bit addresses can only be the 16-bit “data pointer” register, DPTR.

Aside from the MUL and DIV an instruction, the “B” register is often used as yet another temporary storage register much like a ninth "R" register.

Program Status Word The PSW register contains program status information. It is a 8-bit flag register, out of 8-bits 6 bits are used and 2 bits are reserved. Out of 6 bits 4 bits are conditional bits and 2 bits are used for selecting register bank.

Control Register for the 80C51 Special Function Registers IP, IE, TMOD, TCON, SCON, and PCON contain control and status bits for the interrupt system, the Timer/Counters, and the serial port. Register Banks The 8051 uses 8 "R" registers which are used in many of its instructions. These "R" registers are numbered from 0 through 7 (R0, R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R6, and R7).

Addressing Modes

The CPU can access data in various ways, which are called addressing modes

1. Immediate 2. Register 3. Direct 4.Register indirect 5.Indexed

Immediate Addressing When a source operand is a constant rather than a variable then the constant can be incorporated into the instruction as a byte of "immediate" data. In assembly language, immediate operands are preceded by a number sign (#). The operand may be a numeric constant, a symbolic variable, or an arithmetic expression using constants, symbols, and operators. The assembler computes the value and substitutes the immediate data into the instruction. For example, the instruction

...

Register Indirect Addressing Mode The indirect addressing mode uses a register to hold the actual address that will finally be used in the data move; the register itself is not the address, but rather the number in the register. Indirect addressing for MOV opcodes uses register R0 or R1, often called "data pointers," to hold the address of one of the data locations, which could be a RAM or an SFR address.

1. 8051 OVERVIEW

1.1. Introduction
The 8051 series of microcontrollers are highly integrated single chip microcomputers with an 8-bit CPU, memory, interrupt controller, timers, serial I/O
and digital I/O on a single piece of silicon. The current members of the 8051 family of components include:
80C152JA/JB/JC/JD, 83C152JA/JC, 80C157 80C154, 83C154, 85C154 8044, 8344, 8744 80C451, 83C451, 87C451 80C452, 83C452, 87C452 8051, 8031, 8751, 80C51, 80C31, 87C51 80512, 80532 80515, 80535, 80C535, 80C515 80C517, 80C537 80C51FA, 83C51FA, 87C51FA, 83C51FB, 87C51FB, 83C51FC, 87C51FC 8052, 8032, 8752 80C321, 80C521, 87C521, 80C541, 87C541 8053, 9761, 8753 80C552, 83C552, 87C552 80C652, 83C652, 87C652 83C654, 87C654 83C751, 87C751 83C752, 87C752 80C851, 83C851
All members of the 8051 series of microcontrollers share a common architecture.

...

Its memory is organized in bytes and practically all its instruction deal with byte quantities. It uses an Accumulator as the primary register for instruction results. Other operands can be accessed using one of the four different addressing modes available: register implicit, direct, indirect or immediate. Operands reside in one of the five memory spaces of the 8051. The five memory spaces of the 8051 are: Program Memory, External Data Memory, Internal Data Memory, Special Function Registers and Bit Memory. The Program Memory space contains all the instructions, immediate data and constant tables and strings. It is principally addressed by the 16-bit Program Counter (PC), but it can also be accessed by a few instructions using the 16-bit Data Pointer (DPTR).

...

Data Memory, Special Function Registers and Bit Memory.
The Program Memory space contains all the instructions, immediate data and constant
tables and strings. It is principally addressed by the 16-bit Program Counter (PC), but

## [8051 Architecture – Embedded system](https://ebooks.inflibnet.ac.in/csp13/chapter/8051-architecture/)

4 8051 Architecture

In this lecture the detailed architecture of 8051 controller, register bank, special purpose registers, timers and memory elements of 8051 will be discussed.
1. 8051 Micro controller
The Microcontroller incorporates all the features that are found in microprocessor. It has built in ROM, RAM, Input Output ports, Serial Port, timers, interrupts and clock circuit. Microcontroller (MC) may be called computer on chip since it has basic features within single chip. These are usually dedicated devices embedded within an application.

...

This is widely used in washing machines, vcd player, microwave oven, robotics or in industries. Microcontroller can be classified on the basis of their bits processed like 8bit MC, 16bit MC. 8 bit microcontroller, means it can read, write and process 8 bit data. Ex. 8051 microcontroller. Basically 8 bit specifies the size of data bus. 8 bit microcontroller means 8 bit data can travel on the data bus or we can read, write process 8 bit data.
1.1 8051 Architecture
8051 micro controller is an 8 bit controller. Figure 1.1 shows the architecture diagram of 8051.
The 8051 microcontroller has the following features:
* 4 Kb of ROM.

...

* It has Accumulator, general purpose registers and special purpose registers and
* It has ALU which does all kind of arithmetic and logical operations.
The whole configuration is obviously thought of as to satisfy the needs of most programmers working on development of automation devices. One of its advantages is that nothing is missing and nothing is too much. In other words, it is created exactly in accordance to the average user‘s taste and needs. Another advantages are RAM organization, the operation of Central Processor Unit (CPU) and ports which completely use all recourses and enable further upgrades.
Further it has eight general purpose registers namely R0, R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R6, R7. All are 8 bit wide and used as scratch pad. R0 and R1 are used as pointers in indirect addressing mode. Accumulator is a very important register in 8051. In this figure ACC is the Accumulator register. It is referred as A. It is holding one operand in arithmetic and logical instructions and 8 bit wide.
Next important register is B Register. The B register is used during multiply and divide operations for other instructions it can be treated as another scratch pad register and 8 bit length.
During program execution Program counter (PC) plays vital role. It is 16 bit length. Holds address of the instruction to be execute next. It has many special purpose registers like PSW, TMOD , SBUF etc.
1.2 Program Status Word (PSW)

...

* CY | AC | F0 | RS1 | RS0 | OV | – | P
PSW (Fig 1.2) is a special purpose register. It is 8-bit wide. The PSW register contains program status information execution. It shows the carry Flag and auxiliary carry flag and
* Symbol | Position | Name and significance
* CY | PSW 7 | Carry flag
* AC | PSW 6 | Auxillary carry flag ( For BCD Operations)
* F0 | PSW 5 | Flag 0 (Available to the user for general purposes)

INTRODUCTION TO MICROCONTROLLERS

8051 MICROCONTROLLER:

The Intel 8051 microcontroller is one of the most popular general purpose microcontrollers

in use today. The success of the Intel 8051 spawned a number of clones which are collectively

referred to as the MCS-51 family of microcontrollers, which includes chips from vendors such

as Atmel, Philips, Infineon, and Texas Instruments

...

Some of the features that have made the 8051 popular are:



64 KB on chip program memory.



128 bytes on chip data memory (RAM).



4 register banks.



128 user defined software flags.



8-bit data bus



16-bit address bus



32 general purpose registers each of 8 bits



16 bit timers (usually 2, but may have more, or less).



3 internal and 2 external interrupts.

...

Program Start Address

The 8051 starts executing program instructions from address 0000 in the program memory.

Direct Memory

The 8051 has 256 bytes of internal addressable RAM, although only the first 128 bytes are available for general use by the programmer. The first 128 bytes of RAM (from 0x00 to 0x7F) are called the Direct Memory , and can be used to store data.

Special Function Register

The Special Function Register (SFR) is the upper area of addressable memory, from address 0x80 to 0xFF. A, B, PSW, DPTR are called SFR.This area of memory cannot be used for data or program storage, but is instead a series of memory-mapped ports and registers. All port input and output can therefore be performed by memory mov operations on specified addresses in the SFR. Also, different status registers are mapped into the SFR, for use in checking the status of the 8051, and changing some operational parameters of the 8051.

General Purpose Registers

The 8051 has 4 selectable banks of 8 addressable 8-bit registers, R0 to R7. This means that there are essentially 32 available general purpose registers, although only 8 (one bank) can be directly accessed at a time. To access the other banks, we need to change the current bank number in the flag status register.

A and B Registers

...

In direct addressing, an 8 bit internal data memory address is specified as part of the instruction and hence, it can specify the address only in the range of 00H to FFH. In this addressing mode, data is obtained directly from the memory. Eg. MOV A,60h ADD A,30h 4. Indirect addressing The indirect addressing mode uses a register to hold the actual address that will be used in data movement. Registers R0 and R1 and DPTR are the only registers that can be used as data pointers. Indirect addressing cannot be used to refer to SFR registers. Both R0 and R1 can hold 8 bit address and DPTR can hold16 bit address. Eg. MOV A,@R0 ADD A,@R1 MOVX A,@DPTR 5. Indexed addressing.

Rescuing vintage microcontrollers part 3: Life at long last

Posted on 2 Mar 2026
In this series of posts , I’m rescuing vintage microcontrollers from their decades-long purgatory in a drawer in my local makerspace . To this end, I’m attempting to use them to drive a LED sign made of WS2812 strips
So far in this series , I found some decades-old Signetics SCN8031AH and OKI MSM83C154 microcontrollers in a drawer , and worked out that they’re 8051 and 8052 derivatives (members of the MCS-51 family) from the 1980s, and calculated that it should be possible to make them control modern WS2812 LED strips .

MSM80C154S/83C154S ¡ Semiconductor
GENERAL DESCRIPTION
The MSM80C154S/MSM83C154S, designed for the high speed version of the existing MSM80C154/MSM83C154, is a higher performance 8-bit microcontroller providing low-power consumption. The MSM80C154S/MSM83C154S covers the functions and operating range of the existing MSM80C154/83C154/80C51F/80C31F. The MSM80C154S is identical to the MSM83C154S except it does not contain the internal program memory (ROM).
FEATURES
• Operating range Operating frequency : 0 to 3 MHz (Vcc=2.2 to 6.0 V) 0 to 12 MHz (Vcc=3.0 to 6.0 V) 0 to 24 MHz (Vcc=4.5 to 6.0 V) Operating voltage : 2.2 to 6.0 V Operating temperature : –40 to +85°C (Operation at +125°C conforms to the other specification.) • Fully static circuit • Upward compatible with the MSM80C51F/80C31F • On-chip program memory : 16K words x 8 bits ROM (MSM83C154S only) • On-chip data memory : 256 words x 8 bits RAM • External program memory address space : 64K bytes ROM (Max) • External data memory address space : 64K bytes RAM • I/O ports : 4 ports x 8 bits (Port 1, 2, 3, impedance programmable) : 32 • 16-bit timer/counters : 3 • Multifunctional serial port : I/O Expansion mode : UART mode (featuring error detection) • 6-source 2-priority level Interrupt and multi-level Interrupt available by programming IP and IE registers • Memory-mapped special function registers • Bit addressable data memory and SFRs • Minimum instruction cycle : 500 ns @ 24 MHz operation • Standby functions : Power-down mode (oscillator stop) Activated by software or hardware; providing ports with floating or active status The software power-down stet mode is termi- nated by interrupt signal enabling execution from the interrupted address.

Let's map: For channel n, reading 1 index = E1 + 2*(n-1): n=1 -> E1, n=2 -> E3, n=8 -> EF. Reading 2 index = E0 + 2*(n-1): n=1 -> E0, n=8 -> EE. ### Dump method / EA latch
Datasheet says EA is an input; no explicit statement of latching at reset. The original 8051 **does** latch EA? Let me recall: Intel 8051 EA pin: "External Access enable: EA must be strapped to VSS in order to enable the device to fetch code from external program memory locations 0000H to 0FFFH. If EA is held high, the device executes from internal program memory..." On 8051, EA is **latched during reset**? I recall Atmel AT89C51: "EA is sampled at reset and must be stable..." Actually many 8051 datasheets say EA is latched at reset. The OKI datasheet might say "When EA is held at H level..." suggesting not latched. The dump checksum verifies, so empirically it worked. But the doc says "does not latch EA at reset" as fact; maybe the correct statement is "EA is not latched on this part, so it can be changed after reset" — likely valid. But we can note the datasheet doesn't explicitly say, and the evidence is the successful dump. The dump checksum is strong evidence.

Yet here's a subtlety: The dump procedure raises EA after ~10 ms so 8052 fetches internal ROM at 0000-3FFF while executing code from external at 0x4000. If EA were latched, this wouldn't work. The checksum 0xB945 verifies the ROM content. So yes.

The on-chip firmware's checksum routine would run only if the 8052 is executing internal code after EA high; but it's executing the dumper from external. GENERAL DESCRIPTION 



The MSM83C154/MSM80C154 is a high performance 8-bit one-chip microcontroller implementing large 
integration, high speed and low power consumption by 2 silicon gate CMOS process technology. 
The MSM83C154 features 16K byte ROM, 256 byte RAM, 32 I/O ports, three 16-bit timer/counters, 
multifunctional serial port and clock generator. In addition, the MSM83C154 has three standby modes 
enabling further power reduction. 

The MSM80C154 is identical to the MSM83C154 except the omission of 16K byte ROM.

# **OKI** **semiconductor MSM80C154/ MSM83C154**

**CMOS 8-bit One-Chip Microcontroller**

**GENERAL DESCRIPTION**

The MSMS3C154/MSMSOC154 is a high performance S.lJit one-chip microcontroller implementing large integration, high speed and low power consumption by 2 }.1m silicon gate CMOS process technology. The MSMS3C154 features 16K byte ROM, 256 byte RAM, 32 I/O ports, three 16-bit timer/counters, multifunctional serial port and clock generator. In addition, the MSMS3C154 has three standby modes enabling further power reduction. The MSMSOC154 is identical to the MSMS3C154 except the omission of 16K byte ROM.

**FEATURES**

• Fully static circuit

• On-chip program memory

• On-chip data memory

• External program memory address space

• External data memory address space

• I/O ports (Port 1,2,3, impedance programmable)

• 16.IJit timer/counters (includes watch dog timer & 32 bit timer)

• Multifunctional serial port

• 6-source 2-priority level interrupt and multi-level

## [Rescuing the makerspace's vintage microcontrollers - Jamie Montgomerie’s World Wide Web Log](https://www.blog.montgomerie.net/posts/2026-01-13-rescuing-the-makerspaces-vintage-microcontrollers)
Published: 2026-01-13T00:00:00.000Z

Jamie Montgomerie’s World Wide Web Log
Home Tags All About

Rescuing the makerspace's vintage microcontrollers

Posted on 13 Jan 2026
I recently joined my local makerspace , and one of the exciting 1 things there is this shelf of electronic components, available for all members to use:
A shelf with three sets of Akro-Mills style component drawers. The drawers look old.
I felt a bit like an archeologist going through these. Everything in them, apart from some Arduinos and Raspberry Pi related stuff in the middle shelves, seems to be at least thirty years old! There’s the usual selection of resistors, capacitors, transistors, and other small through-hole components. Among the more complex things, a lot seems to be loosely audio-related - amps, signal generators and the like (I bet someone could make some cool synths!). There are a load of old-school UV-light-erasable EPROMs.
What interested me most, though, was a huge stash of PLCC ICs. Just look at this!
A drawer from one of the cabinets. It has two compartments, each filled with loads of 44-pin PLCC ICs
What are these?
Can I build something with them and finally release them from their component drawer purgatory?

Archeology

In the front section are what look like Signetics chips with these markings:
[Signetics logo] 8450
SCN8031H
CCA44  E
This took a little time to decode. Turns out the part number wraps around - this is an SCN8031HCCA44 . The only other text - 8450 - is likely the date code, suggesting these were produced in week 50 - mid December - of 1984. Here’s a data sheet !
In the back section there are a bunch of OKI ICs, with these markings:
79X1396
M83C154-42
©️OKI '80/85
JAPAN 94000
These seem to be M83C154-42 s. Presuming the date code is 94000 , they were made in January 1994 (although it does seem weirdly ’lucky’ that these were produced in the 0th week of the year!).
It took a bit of time to find the right data sheet for these. OKI seems to have omitted an MS prefix on the part number. And search engines love to return a data sheet for the MSM83C154S - a newer variant 2 . Finally, though, I hit upon this older data sheet specifically for the MSM80C154/MSM83C154 , and this Archive.org copy of OKI’s 1986 ‘Data Book’ , which also contains the data sheet. If these ICs are from 1994, they’re from near the end of the production timespan.

Findings

What did the data sheets tell me?
Both the Signetics SCN8031H and the OKI MSM83C154 are Intel MCS-51 compatible microcontrollers (although the data sheets are strangely coy about this - legal reasons?), with pretty much identical pin-outs.
Unlike basically any modern microcontrollers, neither of these contain any flash ROM. They need the program to be on a separate ROM, connected with an 8- or 16-bit wide bus (depending on how much space you need for your code). This certainly explains all the EPROMs also in the cabinets! 3
The OKI chips are a little better specced than the Signetics ones; 16 vs 12 MHz top speed, 256 bytes of internal RAM vs 128, an extra interrupt, 3 timers (one of them 32 bits!) vs 2. It seems like the OKI chips are more like the Intel 8052, and the Signetics chips are more like the older 8051.
Other capabilities will feel familiar to anyone used to modern microcontrollers. There is a UART (serial port), 32 GPIO pins (or “I/O lines” as the data sheet call them), and various other peripheral functions. The GPIO count drops in practical use though. If you want to use external ROM and/or RAM, this repurposes at least eight pins (and I’ll be required to do this because I’m not going to be sending code to be placed in the ROM during manufacturing…). And, just like on a modern microcontroller, more of the pins get repurposed if you want to connect them to the UART, timer, interrupts etc.
This ‘Logic Symbol’ from the Signetics data sheet sums things up pretty well!
A ‘Logic Symbol’ from the SCN8031 data sheet, illustrating the various inputs and outputs of the IC described above.

OKI's single-chip microcontrollers find wide application in various types of electronic equipment in the consumer and the industrial fields. Our products have been enjoying a good reputation for their high quality and high performance. The most outstanding feature employed in all of OKI's
microcontrollers is CMOS technology which ensures low power operation.
OKI will continue to enhance the its microcontroller series and program development systems to cater to cutomers' requirements.

**GENERAL DESCRIPTION**

The MSM80C154S/MSM83C154S, designed for the high speed version of the existing MSM80C154/MSM83C154, is a higher performance 8-bit microcontroller providing low-power consumption. The MSM80C154S/MSM83C154S covers the functions and operating range of the existing MSM80C154/83C154/80C51F/80C31F. The MSM80C154S is identical to the MSM83C154S except it does not contain the internal program memory (ROM).

Overview
National Semiconductor marks devices sold in order to provide device identification and manufacturing traceability information. The method of presenting the
information marked on the device is dependent on the size of the device package and the area available for marking as well as the nature and specifications of the
device.
The information presented here describes the majority of the device marking a customer will observe. Specific package marking is given on a device by device basis in
our Price & Availablity section of this web site.
The links below discuss general marking conventions to help understand device markings similar to those in the examples to the right.

Date of Manufacture Codes
Unit Date Code:
The unit date code markings are in 4 digits, 3 digits, 2 digits or single digit formats. The 4 digit date code is used mainly for mil-aero devices. The 3 digit date codes is
used for standard commercial devices where the package marking surface is large enough to have all the required marking information. The 2 digit and the single digit
date codes are used on small packages where the marking surface is limited.
Commercial parts:
The custom commercial parts have weekly date code where the date code changes weekly according to the calendar week. The standard commercial parts plus all
small packages have 6 weekly date codes where the date code changes every 6 weeks. Even though the date codes change every 6 weeks, using the NSID, the date
code and the dierun code, the exact date of production start can be traced using National's on-line traceability system.
The 6-weekly date codes are as below.

## [ Device Marking Conventions](https://e2e.ti.com/cfs-file/__key/communityserver-discussions-components-files/196/2004JUN17_5F00_DA_5F00_ICP_5F00_AN.PDF)
Published: 2003-12-18T00:00:00.000Z

Device Marking Conventions

National Semiconductor marks devices sold in order to pro- vide device identification and manufacturing traceablility in- formation. The method of presenting the information marked on the device is dependent on the size of the device package and the area available for marking, as well as the nature and specifications of the device.
The information presented here describes the majority of the device markings a customer will observe. Specific package marking for a given device is given in the datasheet for that device. A package may have up to four lines of marking. The following information is usually contained in each line.
First line: Manufacturing information • Company logo • Wafer and/or assembly plant codes (optional) (see Table 1. Wafer Fab Plant Code and Table 2. Assembly Plant Code ) • Date code (see Table 3. Year Code , Table 4. Six-Week Period Code , and Table 5. Date Code Examples ) • Die run (wafer lot) code
Second Line: Device part number • Device family (see Table 6. Device Family ) • Device type • Options • Package code (see Table 7. Package Type ) Third or fourth line: Optional, depending on device, package size, and customer • Continuation of device identification (if too long for the second line) • “Stampoff” number as required by specific customer re- quest and specification • Notice(s) related to copyright or trademarks Very small packages, such as SOT-23, SOT-223, SC70, and SC90, are too small to contain all the information discussed above. Device identification marking is assigned differently, consisting of a four-character code: • Device type (see Table 9. Device Type Code ) • Device identification code • Grade
These small packages also have a date code mark on the underside of the package. This is a one-character alpha code that represents a particular 6-week period during a 3-year span.
The specific marking for a given device can be found in the device datasheet. Other date code information, which would be typically found in the “first line” marking, is identified on the container labels.
Figure 1 , Figure 2 , and Figure 3 show the typical arrange- ment of marking on large, medium, and very small pack- ages.

...

Date of Manufacture Codes

Marks indicating the date of manufacture occur in four, three, two, or one digit versions. The date code represents a six- week period in which the device was assembled. The one- digit code is an alpha code for the very small packages, such as SOT, SC70, and SC90, and ranges from A to Z plus the character @, representing a 6-week period during a 3-year span. For the four, three, and two digit codes, the allocation of digits between year and week information in each scheme is summarized in Table 3. Year Code :
TABLE 3. Year Code
Version Year Digits Week Range Digits
Four-digit (YYWW) 2 2
Three-digit (YWW) 1 2
Two-digit (YW) 1 1
Year: The year code is the last one or two digits of the calendar year of manufacture.

## [Japanese Semiconductor Terminology and Cross-Reference Guide for Component Engineers | Engineering Guide | IC Online | IC Online](https://www.ic-online.com/blog/post/japanese-semiconductor-terminology-and-cross-reference-guide-for-component-engineers)

* Package code (surface-mount) | FM (Toshiba), TL (Rohm), S (Sanken), PT (Renesas) | SOT-23, SC-70, SOT-89, etc. | “FM” = SOT-23 or mini-mold (Toshiba). “TL” = SOT-23 (Rohm). Renesas “PT” = SC-59. Always verify dimensions.
* Lot number format | Alphanumeric, often 4–5 digits | Date code + plant code (JEDEC) | Renesas: 4-digit code (YWWx). Rohm: 3- or 4-digit separate date mark. Toshiba: lot code may embed year/month. No universal standard.
* Date code | Often embedded in lot number or separate marking | YYWW or YYWWLL (JEDEC) | Sanken uses a 2-digit year + 2-digit week on many discretes. Toshiba may use a single-character year code. Cross-reference the manufacturer’s lot interpretation guide.

...

4. Decode the lot number for traceability. If you’re qualifying a new source or investigating a field failure, you need to know when the part was made. Most Japanese manufacturers encode the production date in the lot number or a separate date code. Renesas often uses a 4-digit alphanumeric code where the first digit represents the year and the second the month (e.g., “3A” could mean 2023, January). Rohm may print a separate 3- or 4-digit date mark. The only reliable way to interpret these codes is to obtain the manufacturer’s lot interpretation guide—usually available through your authorized distributor.

...

* Check Item | What to Look For | Common Pitfall
* h FE rank suffix | Letter code (Y, GR, BL, etc.) in ordering code; gain range in datasheet | Assuming all ranks are interchangeable; circuit bias may shift outside tolerance
* Package code | Manufacturer-specific suffix (TP, FM, TL, etc.); mechanical drawing | Confusing through-hole and surface-mount variants; footprint mismatch
* Tape/reel orientation | Suffix like TE85L, Q, S1; tape width and quantity per reel | Incorrect orientation causes pick-and-place errors; wrong reel size jams feeders
* Lot number / date code | Format per manufacturer’s lot guide; consistency across parts | Assuming JEDEC date code format; missing a lot-specific reliability alert

...

For instance, a 2SC1815-TP is a TO-92 in tape, while a 2SC1815-FM is a surface-mount device in a SOT-23-like package. The mechanical drawings in the datasheet are the final authority.
Q: Are Japanese semiconductor lot numbers traceable to wafer fabrication dates?
Most Japanese manufacturers encode the production date (year/week or year/month) within the lot number or a separate date code, but the format is not standardized. Renesas often uses a 4-digit alphanumeric code, while Rohm may use a separate 3- or 4-digit date mark. Traceability requires the manufacturer’s lot interpretation guide. Authorized distributors can provide these guides and help you decode a specific lot. For high-reliability applications, request a Certificate of Conformance that includes the date code explanation.

Oki Electric Industry MSM531602E

MSM531602E is a high-speed CMOS Mask ROM that can electrically switch between 1,048,576-word x 16-bit or 2,097,152-word x 8-bit configurations. The MSM531602E Operates on a single 5.0V power supply and is TTL compatible. The chip's asynchronous I/O requires no external clock assuring easy operation.

DESCRIPTION

The OKI A power-down mode provides low power dissipation when the chip is not selected. The CE and OE pins are provided as control signals that permit three-stated output allowing easy memory expansion on a system bus.The MSM531602E is suited for use as large capacity fixed memory for microcomputers and data terminals.
